claim: TMEM16A is a member of a conserved protein family that comprises ion channels and lipid scramblases.
source: The calcium-activated chloride channel TMEM16A is a member of a conserved protein family that comprises ion channels and lipid scramblases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work on the family.

claim: The structure of the scramblase nhTMEM16 has defined the architecture of the TMEM16 family.
source: Although the structure of the scramblase nhTMEM16 has defined the architecture of the family, it was unknown how a channel has adapted to cope with its distinct functional properties.
evidence: This refers to prior structural work on nhTMEM16 that established the general fold of the family.

claim: The structure of mouse TMEM16A was determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here we have addressed this question by the structure determination of mouse TMEM16A by cryo-electron microscopy and a complementary functional characterization.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental determination of the structure using cryo-EM.

claim: mTMEM16A shows a similar organization to nhTMEM16, except for changes at the site of catalysis.
source: The protein shows a similar organization to nhTMEM16, except for changes at the site of catalysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing the structural comparison.

claim: The conformation of transmembrane helices constituting a membrane-spanning furrow in scramblases has changed to form an enclosed aqueous pore in TMEM16A.
source: There, the conformation of transmembrane helices constituting a membrane-spanning furrow that provides a path for lipids in scramblases has changed to form an enclosed aqueous pore that is largely shielded from the membrane.
evidence: This describes the key structural difference observed between the channel and scramblase.

claim: Calcium-activated chloride channels are important constituents of diverse physiological processes.
source: Calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) are important constituents of diverse physiological processes, ranging from epithelial chloride secretion to the control of electrical excitability in smooth muscles and neurons (Hartzell et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2012; Oh and Jung, 2016; Pedemonte and Galietta, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: CaCCs are activated upon an increase of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: These ligand-gated ion channels are activated upon an increase of the intracellular Ca2+ concentration as a consequence of cellular signaling events.
evidence: This is a well-established property of calcium-activated chloride channels.

claim: TMEM16A is the best-characterized protein mediating CaCC function.
source: Although CaCC function can be accomplished by unrelated protein architectures (Kane Dickson et al., 2014, Kunzelmann et al., 2009), the so far best-characterized processes are mediated by the protein TMEM16A (Caputo et al., 2008; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational papers on TMEM16A.

claim: The TMEM16 family contains 10 paralogs in mammals.
source: The family is exclusively found in eukaryotes and contains 10 paralogs in mammals that all share considerable sequence homology (Milenkovic et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and reference to a sequence alignment figure.

claim: Only TMEM16A and TMEM16B function as ion channels in the TMEM16 family.
source: Although it was initially anticipated that all TMEM16 proteins would function as anion channels (Hartzell et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2008), it is now generally accepted that only two family members (the closely related TMEM16A and B) are ion channels (Pifferi et al., 2009; Scudieri et al., 2012), whereas most others work as lipid scramblases, which catalyze the passive and bidirectional diffusion of lipids between the two leaflets of a phospholipid bilayer (Brunner et al., 2016; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013, 2010; Whitlock and Hartzell, 2017, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: Most TMEM16 family members work as lipid scramblases.
source: Although it was initially anticipated that all TMEM16 proteins would function as anion channels (Hartzell et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2008), it is now generally accepted that only two family members (the closely related TMEM16A and B) are ion channels (Pifferi et al., 2009; Scudieri et al., 2012), whereas most others work as lipid scramblases, which catalyze the passive and bidirectional diffusion of lipids between the two leaflets of a phospholipid bilayer (Brunner et al., 2016; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013, 2010; Whitlock and Hartzell, 2017, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: Lipid scramblases catalyze the passive and bidirectional diffusion of lipids between the two leaflets of a phospholipid bilayer.
source: whereas most others work as lipid scramblases, which catalyze the passive and bidirectional diffusion of lipids between the two leaflets of a phospholipid bilayer (Brunner et al., 2016; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013, 2010; Whitlock and Hartzell, 2017, 2016).
evidence: This is a definition of lipid scramblase function supported by citations.

claim: The TMEM16 family shows a new protein fold as revealed by the structure of nhTMEM16.
source: The TMEM16 family shows a new protein fold, as revealed by the structure of the fungal homologue nhTMEM16, which functions as lipid scramblase (Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the nhTMEM16 structure paper.

claim: nhTMEM16 consists of structured cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal components and a transmembrane domain containing 10 transmembrane helices.
source: nhTMEM16 consists of structured cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal components and a transmembrane domain (TMD) containing 10 transmembrane helices.
evidence: This describes the structural organization of nhTMEM16 from prior work.

claim: TMEM16 proteins are homo-dimers.
source: As general for the TMEM16 family, the protein is a homo-dimer (Fallah et al., 2011; Sheridan et al., 2011) with each subunit containing its own lipid translocation path located at the two opposite corners of a rhombus-shaped protein distant from the dimer interface (Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biochemical and structural studies.

claim: Each subunit of nhTMEM16 contains its own lipid translocation path.
source: As general for the TMEM16 family, the protein is a homo-dimer (Fallah et al., 2011; Sheridan et al., 2011) with each subunit containing its own lipid translocation path located at the two opposite corners of a rhombus-shaped protein distant from the dimer interface (Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the nhTMEM16 structure.

claim: The lipid translocation path in nhTMEM16 is formed by a membrane-spanning furrow called the subunit cavity.
source: This lipid path is formed by the 'subunit cavity', a membrane-spanning furrow of appropriate size to harbor a lipid headgroup.
evidence: This describes the structural feature of nhTMEM16 that mediates lipid scrambling.

claim: The subunit cavity in nhTMEM16 is exposed to the membrane.
source: Since the subunit cavity is exposed to the membrane, it was proposed that its polar surface provides a favorable environment for lipid headgroups on their way across the membrane, whereas the fatty-acid chains remain embedded in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer (Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of lipid scrambling in nhTMEM16.

claim: A conserved regulatory calcium-binding site controls the activity of TMEM16 proteins.
source: In the vicinity of each subunit cavity, within the membrane-embedded domain, a conserved regulatory calcium-binding site controls the activity of the protein (Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the nhTMEM16 structure and functional studies.

claim: The same region constituting the scrambling path also forms the ion conduction pore in TMEM16A.
source: Previous results suggested that the same region constituting the scrambling path also forms the ion conduction pore (Yang et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies cited.

claim: The structure of mTMEM16A was determined at 6.6 Å resolution by cryo-EM.
source: Here we have resolved this controversy by the structure determination of mouse TMEM16A (mTMEM16A) by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) at 6.6 Å resolution and a complementary electrophysiological characterization of pore mutants.
evidence: This is the main result of the study.

claim: mTMEM16A shows a similar overall fold and dimeric organization as nhTMEM16.
source: The protein shows a similar overall fold and dimeric organization as the lipid scramblase nhTMEM16.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Conformational rearrangements of helices lining the lipid scrambling path have sealed the subunit cavity in mTMEM16A.
source: However, conformational rearrangements of helices lining the lipid scrambling path have sealed the subunit cavity, resulting in the formation of a protein-enclosed ion conduction pore that is for most parts shielded from the membrane but that might be partly accessible to lipids on its intracellular side.
evidence: This is the key structural finding from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ion conduction pore in mTMEM16A is protein-enclosed and largely shielded from the membrane.
source: However, conformational rearrangements of helices lining the lipid scrambling path have sealed the subunit cavity, resulting in the formation of a protein-enclosed ion conduction pore that is for most parts shielded from the membrane but that might be partly accessible to lipids on its intracellular side.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ion conduction pore in mTMEM16A might be partly accessible to lipids on its intracellular side.
source: However, conformational rearrangements of helices lining the lipid scrambling path have sealed the subunit cavity, resulting in the formation of a protein-enclosed ion conduction pore that is for most parts shielded from the membrane but that might be partly accessible to lipids on its intracellular side.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structure.

claim: A stable HEK293 cell-line constitutively expressing mTMEM16A(ac) was generated.
source: We were interested in the structural properties that distinguish ion channels from lipid scramblases in the TMEM16 family and thus decided to investigate the structural properties of the chloride channel TMEM16A by single particle cryo-EM. For that purpose, we generated a stable HEK293 cell-line, which constitutively expresses the (ac) isoform of mTMEM16A, and purified the protein at a saturating calcium concentration in the detergent digitonin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for protein production.

claim: mTMEM16A was purified at a saturating calcium concentration in the detergent digitonin.
source: For that purpose, we generated a stable HEK293 cell-line, which constitutively expresses the (ac) isoform of mTMEM16A, and purified the protein at a saturating calcium concentration in the detergent digitonin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the purification conditions.

claim: The three-dimensional structure of mTMEM16A was reconstructed from 213,243 particles picked from 4178 micrographs.
source: The three-dimensional structure of the mammalian ion channel at a nominal resolution of 6.6 Å was reconstructed from total of 213,243 particles picked from 4178 micrographs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; and Table 1).
evidence: This describes the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The resolution of the mTMEM16A structure is likely limited by the sample.
source: Since the resolution did not significantly improve after addition of further images, it is likely limited by the sample.
evidence: This is an inference from the data processing results.

claim: The main features of mTMEM16A are well defined in the electron density map.
source: In the resulting electron density map, the main features of the protein are well defined (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: Similarities with nhTMEM16 allowed the construction of a poly-alanine model of mTMEM16A.
source: Similarities with nhTMEM16 allowed the construction of a poly-alanine model encompassing the secondary structure elements of the TMD and most of the cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This describes the model building approach.

claim: The structure likely shows mTMEM16A in a Ca2+-bound conformation.
source: Due to the presence of Ca2+, it likely shows the channel in a Ca2+-bound conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the purification conditions.

claim: It is ambiguous whether the mTMEM16A structure corresponds to a conducting or non-conducting state.
source: In light of the irreversible rundown of TMEM16A-mediated currents observed in patch-clamp experiments at high Ca2+ concentrations, it is at this point ambiguous whether this conformation corresponds to a conducting or a non-conducting state of the channel.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the functional state of the structure.

claim: The overall dimensions of mTMEM16A within the membrane are very similar to nhTMEM16.
source: Within the membrane, the overall dimensions of mTMEM16A are very similar to nhTMEM16 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and Video 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: All transmembrane helices of mTMEM16A are well resolved and could be unambiguously allocated.
source: All transmembrane helices are well resolved and thus, could be unambiguously allocated.
evidence: This describes the quality of the structure.

claim: The mTMEM16A map contains unassigned density on the extracellular side that can be attributed to extended loops.
source: On the extracellular side, the mTMEM16A map contains a substantial amount of unassigned density that can be attributed to extended loops connecting transmembrane α-helices 1–2 (α1α2 loop) and transmembrane α-helices 9–10 (α9α10 loop), which are respectively 50 and 65 residues longer compared to nhTMEM16 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM map and sequence comparison.

claim: The extracellular loops of mTMEM16A appear to be structured and fold into a compact extracellular domain.
source: Both loops appear to be structured, folding into a compact extracellular domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM density.

claim: The extracellular domain of mTMEM16A harbors six cysteines that are indispensable for channel activity.
source: Notably, this domain harbors six cysteines that have been shown to be indispensable for channel activity (Yu et al., 2012) and that are thus potentially involved in disulfide bridges.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies and structural inference.

claim: The N-terminal domain of mTMEM16A exhibits a similar fold and location to nhTMEM16.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, the N-terminal domain of mTMEM16A exhibits a similar fold and location with respect to the TMD as its counterpart in nhTMEM16 (Figures 1B and 2B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: There is no interaction between the N-terminal domains of adjacent subunits in mTMEM16A.
source: Consequently, there is no interaction between the N-terminal domains of adjacent subunits, which was previously proposed based on biochemical experiments (Tien et al., 2013).
evidence: This structural observation contradicts a prior hypothesis.

claim: A 92 residue long extension preceding the folded N-terminal domain of mTMEM16A appears to be unstructured.
source: A 92 residue long extension in mTMEM16A that precedes the folded N-terminal domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) appears to be unstructured, but there is unaccounted electron density that cannot be interpreted at the current resolution of the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This is based on the absence of clear density for this region.

claim: The first α-helix of the C-terminus (Cα1) in mTMEM16A is folded but has moved away from the dimer axis.
source: At the C-terminus, which is 38 residues shorter than its equivalent part in nhTMEM16, the first α-helix (Cα1) is folded but it has moved away from the dimer axis and thus no longer contacts its symmetry mate (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with nhTMEM16.

claim: The remainder of the C-terminus in mTMEM16A is likely unstructured and does not interact with the adjacent subunit.
source: The remainder of the C-terminus is likely unstructured and, unlike in nhTMEM16, does not interact with the adjacent subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density and comparison with nhTMEM16.

claim: The interaction of subunits within the mTMEM16A dimer differs significantly from nhTMEM16.
source: Hence, the interaction of the subunits within the mTMEM16A dimer differs significantly from nhTMEM16 since the cytosolic domains do not contribute to the dimer interface.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Interactions between subunits in mTMEM16A are established mainly at the extracellular part of transmembrane α-helix 10.
source: Instead, interactions are established mainly at the extracellular part of transmembrane α-helix 10, which is in a similar location as in nhTMEM16 but extends further towards the outside (Figures 1 and 2D).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: All membrane-spanning segments of mTMEM16A are well defined in the TMD.
source: In the TMD, all membrane-spanning segments are well defined including two short amphiphilic α-helices at its N-terminal part that interact with the polar headgroups at the inner leaflet of the lipid bilayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This describes the quality of the structure.

claim: The transmembrane helices of mTMEM16A are in comparable locations to their counterparts in nhTMEM16.
source: In general, the transmembrane helices are in comparable locations to their counterparts in nhTMEM16 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and thus account for the overall similarity between both structures.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The pore region of mTMEM16A is formed by transmembrane α-helices 3–8.
source: The pore region of mTMEM16A, also containing the regulatory calcium-binding site, is formed by transmembrane α-helices 3–8.
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The pore region of mTMEM16A is well defined, except for the loops connecting α-helices 5 and 6 and 6 and 6'.
source: This region is well defined, except for the loops connecting α-helices 5 and 6 and 6 and 6' (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This describes the quality of the structure in the pore region.

claim: The placement of residues in the pore region is facilitated by conserved loops connecting α-helices 4–5, 7–8 and 8–9.
source: The placement is facilitated by conserved loops connecting α-helices 4–5, 7–8 and 8–9, which are well defined in the cryo-EM map and thus determine the register of the transmembrane segments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes how the model was built.

claim: The position of the conserved calcium-binding site in mTMEM16A was constrained by density between α-helices 6, 7 and 8.
source: We could further constrain the position of the conserved calcium-binding site, as density between α-helices 6, 7 and 8 coincides with the position of the two bound calcium ions of nhTMEM16 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the nhTMEM16 structure.

claim: The ion conduction pore in mTMEM16A is lined by residues located on α-helices 3–7.
source: The ion conduction pore is lined by residues located on α-helices 3–7 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: Several of the pore-forming α-helices in mTMEM16A have changed their position relative to nhTMEM16.
source: In contrast to the transmembrane segments close to the dimer interface (i.e. α-helices 1, 2, 9, 10), several of the pore-forming α-helices have changed their position relative to nhTMEM16 (Figures 1B and 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The conformational changes are most pronounced for α-helices 3, 4 and 6 in mTMEM16A.
source: These changes are most pronounced for α-helices 3, 4 and 6.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: α4 and α6 have come into contact at the extracellular part of the membrane to form a protein-enclosed conduit in mTMEM16A.
source: As a consequence of conformational rearrangements, α4 and α6, which line the opposite borders of the membrane-accessible subunit cavity of nhTMEM16, have come into contact at the extracellular part of the membrane to form a protein-enclosed conduit that is shielded from lipids (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is the key structural finding explaining the difference between channels and scramblases.

claim: α-helices 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 constitute the narrow neck of an aqueous pore that spans the extracellular two thirds of the membrane in mTMEM16A.
source: Together with α-helices 3, 5 and 7, they constitute the narrow neck of an aqueous pore that spans the extracellular two thirds of the membrane (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 3).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The detachment of α4 and α6 results in a dilation of the pore to a wide intracellular vestibule in mTMEM16A.
source: Towards the intracellular side, the detachment of α4 and α6 results in the a dilation of the pore to a wide intracellular vestibule that is exposed to both the cytoplasm and the lipid bilayer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The gap between α4 and α6 may cause a local destabilization of the membrane in mTMEM16A.
source: The resulting gap between both α-helices may cause a local destabilization of the membrane that is also manifested in a distortion of the detergent micelle observed in the density at lower contour (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure and the observed micelle distortion.

claim: The narrow upper part of the pore most likely requires permeating ions to shed their hydration shell.
source: Under the assumption that the structure is close to a conducting state, the narrow upper part most likely requires permeating ions to shed their hydration shell.
evidence: This is inferred from the pore geometry.

claim: The anion selectivity of TMEM16A follows a type 1 Eisenman sequence.
source: This is consistent with the observation that the anion selectivity of TMEM16A follows a type 1 Eisenman sequence (Qu and Hartzell, 2000; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008), which favors larger anions with a lower solvation energy.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies.

claim: The pore of mTMEM16A is amphiphilic and contains charged, polar and apolar residues.
source: The pore is amphiphilic and contains charged, polar and apolar residues.
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The low effective affinity of Cl- conduction suggests weak interactions with permeating ions.
source: The low effective affinity of Cl- conduction suggests weak interactions with permeating ions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on functional measurements.

claim: The mutation K588A has resulted in a strong outward rectification of the current.
source: In the model of mTMEM16A, this residue is located at the end of the funnel-shaped vestibule close to the neck of the ion conduction path (Figure 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). In our data, the mutation K588A has resulted in a similar rectification, indicating that the truncation of the positively charged side-chain has perturbed the electrostatic interaction with permeating anions, (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C) effectively increasing the energy barrier of negatively charged ions to enter the pore from its intracellular side (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The mutation K645A has resulted in outward rectification similar to K588A.
source: A similar effect was observed for the nearby mutant K645A, which removes a positive charge from α-helix six at a position that is located slightly further towards the extracellular side (Figure 5A,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Several mutations of positively charged residues located in the wide intracellular vestibule did not alter the linear current-voltage relationship of WT.
source: In contrast, several mutations of positively charged residues located in the wide intracellular vestibule did not alter the linear current-voltage relationship of WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The mutation R535A has resulted in an inward-rectification.
source: At the opposite end of the pore, the mutation R535A has resulted in an inward-rectification, indicating that the mutation hampers the entrance of the anion from the outside (Figure 5A,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The mutation R515A has caused a deviation from the linear current-voltage relationship in both directions.
source: In between Lys 645 and Arg 535, the mutation R515A has caused a deviation from the linear current-voltage relationship in both directions (Figure 5A,E).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: R515 most likely lowers a rate-limiting energy barrier for anion permeation halfway through the narrow part of the mTMEM16A pore.
source: Thus, this positive charge most likely lowers a rate-limiting energy barrier for anion permeation halfway through the narrow part of the mTMEM16A pore (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data.

claim: The mutation R515A results in six-fold lower currents despite robust expression at the cell surface.
source: This is consistent with the six-fold lower currents measured for this mutant, despite its robust expression at the surface of HEK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology and imaging experiments.

claim: No single positive charge dominates the strong anion selectivity of TMEM16A.
source: In no case have we seen any change in the reversal potential measured in asymmetric chloride concentrations, which indicates that no single positive charge dominates the strong anion selectivity of the channel (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The electrophysiology data support the notion of a narrow pore in TMEM16A that widens towards the intracellular side.
source: Together with our structural investigations, the electrophysiology data support the notion of a narrow pore in TMEM16A that widens towards the intracellular side.
evidence: This is a conclusion from combining structural and functional data.

claim: The general architecture of each subunit is shared between TMEM16 channels and scramblases.
source: As anticipated from the strong sequence conservation, the general architecture of each subunit is shared between both branches of the family (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The mTMEM16A structure provides proof for a double barreled channel with two pores, each contained within a single subunit.
source: Although this hypothesis was already refuted by recent functional investigations, which demonstrated that the protein contains two ion conduction pores that are independently activated by Ca2+ (Jeng et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2016), the ultimate proof for a double barreled channel is now provided by the mTMEM16A structure, which reveals the location of two pores, each contained within a single subunit of the dimeric protein.
evidence: This is based on the structure and prior functional studies.

claim: The study provides strong evidence against the proteolipidic pore hypothesis.
source: Our study has also provided strong evidence against this hypothesis. Instead, the model of mTMEM16A shows that α-helical rearrangements have resulted in occlusion of the lipid pathway, while opening up a conductive pore which is largely shielded from the membrane (Figure 6 and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The only potential access of lipids to the pore is provided on the intracellular side where α-helices 4 and 6 detach.
source: The only potential access of lipids is provided on the intracellular side where the detachment of transmembrane α-helices 4 and 6 form a funnel-shaped vestibule that is exposed to the cytoplasm and the lipid bilayer (Figures 5A and 6B).
evidence: This is based on the structure.

claim: The gap between α4 and α6 may be a relic of an ancestral scramblase.
source: The gap between both α-helices may be a relic of an ancestral scramblase, and as suggested by the observed distortion of the detergent micelle in mTMEM16A, possibly destabilizes the bilayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structure.

claim: A similar gap is present in nhTMEM16 where membrane-bending has been proposed to facilitate scramblase activity.
source: Notably, this gap is also present in nhTMEM16, where a similar effect of membrane-bending has been proposed to facilitate scramblase activity, as suggested by molecular dynamics simulations (Bethel and Grabe, 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior computational studies.

claim: The intracellular region connecting transmembrane α-helices 4 and 5 plays an important role in lipid scrambling in TMEM16F.
source: In this respect, it is noteworthy that the intracellular region connecting transmembrane α-helices 4 and 5 has recently been identified to play an important role in lipid scrambling in TMEM16F and was thus assigned the term 'scramblase domain' (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies.

claim: TMEM16A itself does not facilitate lipid transport.
source: Whereas TMEM16A itself does not facilitate lipid transport, scrambling activity was conferred to a chimeric TMEM16A protein carrying the 'scramblase domain' of TMEM16F (Yu et al., 2015) or the equivalent region of TMEM16E (Gyobu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies.

claim: Scrambling activity was conferred to a chimeric TMEM16A protein carrying the 'scramblase domain' of TMEM16F.
source: Whereas TMEM16A itself does not facilitate lipid transport, scrambling activity was conferred to a chimeric TMEM16A protein carrying the 'scramblase domain' of TMEM16F (Yu et al., 2015) or the equivalent region of TMEM16E (Gyobu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies.

claim: The altered structure of the 'subunit cavity' in TMEM16A leaves the mechanism of lipid scrambling in chimeras ambiguous.
source: Although these results emphasize the general role of the intracellular funnel region for lipid interactions, the altered structure of the 'subunit cavity', in particular the absence of a membrane-exposed polar crevice in TMEM16A, leave the mechanism of lipid scrambling in these chimeras ambiguous.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structure and prior functional studies.

claim: Permeating anions have to shed their hydration shell and interact with pore-lining residues in mTMEM16A.
source: Assuming that the imaged protein conformation resembles a conducting state, its pore structure suggests that permeating anions have to shed their hydration shell and interact with pore-lining residues (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the pore structure.

claim: There might not be a single strong site for ion coordination in TMEM16A, but ions might weakly interact with the extended pore region.
source: The low effective affinity of Cl- conduction indicates that there might not be a single strong site for ion coordination, but that the ions might instead weakly interact with the extended pore region (Qu and Hartzell, 2000) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from functional data.

claim: No single mutation was identified that weakened the strong selectivity for anions over cations in TMEM16A.
source: This is consistent with the fact that no single mutation was identified so far that weakened the strong selectivity for anions over cations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Ion conduction in TMEM16 scramblases differs significantly from the selective anion permeation in TMEM16 channels.
source: Although ion conduction was previously also reported for TMEM16 family members which function as lipid scramblases (Lee et al., 2016; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2015), it was proposed that these processes are leaks accompanying the movement of lipids (Yu et al., 2015), which differs significantly from the selective anion permeation described here for TMEM16 channels.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies and the current work.

claim: A hydrophilic membrane-exposed cavity in TMEM16 scramblases has changed to an aqueous membrane-shielded pore in TMEM16 channels.
source: Both structures, namely the scramblase nhTMEM16 and the ion channel mTMEM16A, define the structural relationships within the family, whereby a hydrophilic membrane-exposed cavity in TMEM16 scramblases has changed to an aqueous membrane-shielded pore in TMEM16 channels (Figure 6B and Video 4).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the structural comparison.

claim: TMEM16A shares its mechanism for ion conduction with other, structurally unrelated, channel proteins.
source: Despite the unusual functional breadth of the family, this ligand-gated ion channel turns out to share its mechanism for ion conduction with other, structurally unrelated, channel proteins.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the mechanism of ion conduction.
